title: Attach polynomial generators with prescribed compatible faces and fixed degeneracies
statement:
Let $A\to B$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings, let $n\geq0$, and let $P$ be an augmented $n$-truncated simplicial $A$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-coskeleton]. Suppose there are finite sets $E_0,\ldots,E_n$ and specified identifications with polynomial algebras [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]
$$P_k=A[x_{e,\sigma}: e\in E_j,\ 0\leq j\leq k,\ \sigma:[k]\twoheadrightarrow[j]]\quad(0\leq k\leq n),$$
under which every degeneracy operator associated to a surjection $\tau:[\ell]\twoheadrightarrow[k]$ sends $x_{e,\sigma}$ to $x_{e,\sigma\tau}$. Let $T$ be a finite set. For each $t\in T$ prescribe $b_t\in B$ and $a_{t,i}\in P_n$ for $0\leq i\leq n+1$ such that every $a_{t,i}$ augments to $b_t$ and, when $n\geq1$, $d_i a_{t,j}=d_{j-1}a_{t,i}$ for $i<j$. There is an augmented $(n+1)$-truncated simplicial $A$-algebra $P'$ whose restriction is the specified $P$, whose new term is
$$P'_{n+1}=A[x_{e,\sigma}:e\in E_j,\ 0\leq j\leq n,\ \sigma:[n+1]\twoheadrightarrow[j]][y_t:t\in T],$$
and whose new generators satisfy $d_i y_t=a_{t,i}$ and $\epsilon(y_t)=b_t$. Every degeneracy, including the new ones, acts on the displayed polynomial generators by composition of surjections, so this is the same kind of presentation with $E_{n+1}=T$. All simplicial identities and augmentation identities hold.

proof.text: Put $m=n+1$ and $z_e=x_{e,\mathrm{id}_{[j]}}\in P_j$ for $e\in E_j$. Write $P(\alpha)$ for the operator of the given truncated functor. The hypothesis on degeneracies gives $x_{e,\rho}=P(\rho)(z_e)$ for every surjection $\rho:[k]\twoheadrightarrow[j]$, $k\leq n$. Form the displayed polynomial algebra $Q$ in the statement. Define $D_i:Q\to P_n$ on its variables by $D_i(x_{e,\sigma})=P(\sigma\delta_i)(z_e)$ and $D_i(y_t)=a_{t,i}$. This is well-typed: $\sigma\delta_i:[n]\to[j]$ has both degrees at most $n$. Define $S_l:P_n\to Q$ by $S_l(x_{e,\rho})=x_{e,\rho\sigma_l}$. Existence and uniqueness of all these $A$-algebra maps are the polynomial universal property; retain every map in lower degrees.

source.place: Tag 08PX (proposition-polynomial), inductive step; compatible split-generator replacement, using simplicial.tex Tag 017P (definition-split).

proof.text: Check the new face–face relation for $n\geq1$. On $y_t$, $d_iD_j=d_{j-1}D_i$ is precisely the assumed equation $d_i a_{t,j}=d_{j-1}a_{t,i}$. On $x_{e,\sigma}$ its sides are $P(\sigma\delta_j\delta_i)(z_e)$ and $P(\sigma\delta_i\delta_{j-1})(z_e)$ by functoriality in the old truncation. The two increasing maps into $[m]$ omit exactly the same two vertices $i,j$ and hence are equal. The maps agree on coefficients as well, so polynomial uniqueness proves their equality. When $n=0$ this relation has no nonnegative target degree.

source.place: Tag 08PX (proposition-polynomial), inductive step; compatible split-generator replacement, using simplicial.tex Tag 017P (definition-split).

proof.text: Check the new mixed identities on each generator $x_{e,\rho}$ of $P_n$. The value of $D_iS_l$ is $P(\rho\sigma_l\delta_i)(z_e)$. Directly from the maps that omit $i$ and repeat $l$, $\sigma_l\delta_i$ equals $\delta_i\sigma_{l-1}$ if $i<l$, the identity if $i=l,l+1$, and $\delta_{i-1}\sigma_l$ if $i>l+1$. In the first and last cases both intermediate degrees are $n-1$ and $n$, so old functoriality identifies this value with $s_{l-1}d_i(x_{e,\rho})$ or $s_l d_{i-1}(x_{e,\rho})$ respectively; in the middle cases it is $x_{e,\rho}$. These pointwise identities follow by evaluating below, at, and above the repeated vertex. Polynomial uniqueness proves the mixed identities as algebra maps. For $n=0$ only the two middle cases occur.

source.place: Tag 08PX (proposition-polynomial), inductive step; compatible split-generator replacement, using simplicial.tex Tag 017P (definition-split).

proof.text: The only new degeneracy–degeneracy identities have source $P_{n-1}$, so assume $n\geq1$. Applied to $x_{e,\rho}$, the two maps $S_i s_j$ and $S_{j+1}s_i$ for $i\leq j$ give $x_{e,\rho\sigma_j\sigma_i}$ and $x_{e,\rho\sigma_i\sigma_{j+1}}$. The two ordinal surjections agree: collapsing positions $i,i+1$ and then $j,j+1$ is the same ordered quotient as first collapsing $j+1,j+2$ and then $i,i+1$ (for $i=j$ both collapse the same three consecutive vertices). Thus the labels agree. Polynomial uniqueness gives the identity on $P_{n-1}$. All identities lying wholly in old degrees already hold.

source.place: Tag 08PX (proposition-polynomial), inductive step; compatible split-generator replacement, using simplicial.tex Tag 017P (definition-split).

proof.text: The preceding three checks give every retained simplicial identity. Apply the truncated recognition theorem with $N=m$ in the category of commutative $A$-algebras. It gives the required truncated functor, and uniqueness identifies its restriction with the specified $P$, since all old objects and operators were retained. The theorem also expresses every surjection as codegeneracies; composing their prescribed substitutions gives $x_{e,\sigma}\mapsto x_{e,\sigma\tau}$. There is no surjection out of a retained degree strictly larger than $m$, so no degeneracy out of a new $y_t$ needs specification. Set $E_m=T$, with $y_t=x_{t,\mathrm{id}_{[m]}}$.

Define $\epsilon_Q:Q\to B$ by $x_{e,\sigma}\mapsto\epsilon_j(z_e)$ and $y_t\mapsto b_t$. On an old variable, $\epsilon_nD_i(x_{e,\sigma})=\epsilon_j(z_e)$ because the old augmentation commutes with $P(\sigma\delta_i)$; on $y_t$ this is the hypothesis $\epsilon_n(a_{t,i})=b_t$. Also $\epsilon_Q S_l(x_{e,\rho})=\epsilon_j(z_e)=\epsilon_n(x_{e,\rho})$. Polynomial uniqueness proves these augmentation equalities on the whole algebras. The natural-transformation clause of recognition now makes the old augmentation together with $\epsilon_Q$ an augmentation to the constant $B$. This includes $n=0$, where the equality of both augmented faces replaces a degree $-1$ face–face equation. The variables of $Q$ are exactly those demanded, including empty $T$ or empty $E_j$; no domain, nonzero-ring, or Noetherian assumption was used.
